title: Silicon Valley parents want the tech they help build out of their children’s schools
summary:
Both private and public schools in tech regions are limiting the use of tech in classrooms. But will low-income districts be able to follow suit?

full_text:
German Gil spends most of his waking hours looking at screens. Since moving to the San Francisco Bay Area in 2015, the software engineer has bounced between startups and giants including Netflix, Facebook and GitHub.

But when it came to the education of his daughter, Victoria, he wanted her to have a different experience, one in which his “kid could be a kid”.

Gil and his wife enrolled Victoria at the San Francisco Waldorf school, a private school built around nature-based play. Now in fourth grade, Victoria spends her school days free of screens. Instead of working on Chromebooks, the students in her class are binding books by hand.

This sort of experience doesn’t come cheap. Kindergarten tuition at the school, which sits in San Francisco’s affluent Pacific Heights neighborhood, just two miles from the headquarters of the AI giant Anthropic, runs $40,000 a year; high school, close to $60,000. But the program is intensely popular.

It may seem a contradiction, but in the past years, many well-paid tech workers in Silicon Valley have paid a premium to keep their children away from the platforms they help build. Applications for early childhood enrollment at San Francisco Waldorf have grown notably, according to the school’s executive director, Lauren Smith, and many of the new parents work in tech.

Now, parents in the region are pushing for changes beyond private school campuses to public districts, where screens have become a ubiquitous part of life in the classroom. Parents in California tech enclaves such as Mountain View, San Mateo and others want public schools to re-embrace the emphasis on human connection over screen time that schools like San Francisco Waldorf offer. They are organizing, and they are making a dent, with some public schools banning phones or rolling back their use of computer-based tests and assignments.

As evidence mounts of the damage social media and other platforms do to young people – and as courts have begun to agree – parents and governments, have started to re-evaluate kids’ relationship with tech, and its role in education. Major US school districts such as New York City and Los Angeles have recently embraced tech rollbacks. Parents in other countries, too, are increasingly scrutinizing tech’s encroachment into education.

“There is much more buzz around this today than there was a few years ago,” said David Monahan, campaign director of Fairplay, a US advocacy organization fighting to limit screen use among children.

Silicon Valley parents bring something to this fight that many other communities don’t have: firsthand knowledge of the industry. When San Mateo union high school district put together a taskforce last year to examine the role of AI in schools, at least two of its volunteer members worked at large tech companies, including one in Google’s AI division, according to Jennifer Jacobsen, a school board trustee.

“These professionals know more than the average community member about the products,” Jacobsen said. “They can see a longer runway of where these products are headed and their potential impact on education.”

Many American public-school parents are dismayed to learn how early screens enter the classroom.

Jillian Kolongowski, a writer in San Mateo, was stunned when her five-year-old daughter was sent home with a Chromebook for math practice. “I was like, what?! She’s in kindergarten!” Kolongowski recalled.

Candice Wei, a Palo Alto college counselor, was similarly shocked to learn that her kindergarten-age son was using screens in class with few guardrails. It prompted her to dig deeper into what local high schools allow. “YouTube isn’t banned. Generative AI isn’t banned. It’s almost criminally negligent,” she said. “I don’t allow this in my house. Why is it allowed in schools?”

In its early days, ed tech was viewed as a sign of a more equitable and accessible digital future. The pandemic made it an essential part of remote learning, and many tools stayed once students returned to classrooms. In 2025, 99% of schoolteachers surveyed by the New York Times said that their students received school-issued devices, and 81% said that their school gives students screens by kindergarten.

But experts, and a growing number of parents, are worried about the omnipresence of tech in day-to-day learning. Half of US teens spend four or more hours a day on screens, not counting schoolwork. Monahan, of Fairplay, sees classroom screen time as reinforcing those trends. “What sorts of habits are we fostering at school if students spend hours staring at screens with the seal of approval of their teacher?” he asked.

Research suggests that students retain what they learn with pen and paper better than what they learn on screens. Critics also say excessive ed tech replaces, or at least stunts, the student–teacher bond that is critical to emotional learning and strips away the productive struggle that fosters learning.

“You as a human being are much more likely to put in effort for a teacher you love or a parent you love than for a computer that is not really going to give you love,” explained Yvonne Kao, senior director of learning sciences and technology at the nonpartisan educational research non-profit WestEd.

Kao points out that the use of technology can vary widely across US school districts. She describes hearing about rural districts that lack the staff to vet technology or keep up with best practices for buying it.

Silicon Valley parents are in a different position: “There’s a savviness around tech that I think you acquire from being immersed in the tech environment,” Kao said. “You know better what it is good for and what it is bad for, and you can kind of try to thread the needle.”

It’s pushed many in the arms of private schools. Unbound by state and local bureaucracy, private schools in California are able to more quickly change direction, are free to enact policies that limit tech and have more money to spend on teachers instead of apps.

Wei, who started her local chapter of the parent advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, said classroom screen time was an increasingly common cause for leaving the public system that she hears about. “I’ve been approached by parents who considered [our public school], toured it, saw kids on screens, and were like, ‘I guess I’m going private,’” she said.

But it has motivated others like her to push public school districts to vet the companies landing multimillion-dollar contracts with schools and to demand proof that their products improve learning. “That means asking for data about what specific outcomes they’re looking for that this tech is supposed to help with, and knowing what the plan is if they aren’t seeing those outcomes,” said Kolongowski , whose husband works for an AI company. “A lot of these companies have really sexy pitches, but then on the ground, the work doesn’t quite bear out.”

Amid pressure from parents, public schools in San Mateo have stopped sending Chromebooks home with students in kindergarten through second grade, and high schoolers are subject to a blanket ban on cellphones. In Mountain View, schools are moving away from using i-Ready, an adaptive reading and math program used in school districts across California that has drawn criticism for repetitive lessons and been accused of sharing students’ data without consent. A spokesperson for Curriculum Associates, the company behind iReady, said it is committed to student data privacy. “The claims in this litigation are without merit: we do not sell student data, use it for advertising, or create commercial profiles of students. All use of student information is limited to supporting the educational services requested and authorized by schools and districts in compliance with applicable federal and state laws.” Palo Alto public schools, meanwhile, have prohibited the use of a technology developed just next door in Silicon Valley: “smart” glasses.

While proponents of human-centered learning are heartened by the progress, they are concerned that less-resourced districts will be left behind, stuck with the digital learning tools wealthier ones are abandoning.

The “techlash” is broad, said Jon Valant, director of the Brown Center on Education Policy, and parents across income levels want the same thing – high-quality, human-to-human education – for their kids. The difference is who can pay for it. Staff salaries are the biggest expense at any school, Valant explained: “The reason [private schools] cost a lot of money is that they have a lot of adults in those buildings … It’s when budgets get tight that the temptation to replace people with technology is especially hard to resist.”

The gap could only widen: the Trump administration has thrown its weight behind school choice programs, which give families some or all of the public money that would have been spent on their child’s education through vouchers or education savings accounts to use on private schooling. It means that when parents take their children our of public schools and into the private system, they take the funding with them.

“I am worried about this technology rolling out in ways that are very unequal across communities,” Valant said. “What we end up seeing is it’s the kids who are in the lowest-income areas that find themselves spending a whole lot more time on screens, even if their parents don’t want them to be.”

San Francisco Waldorf offers financial aid to families who can’t afford the price tag. But Antero Garcia, a professor at Stanford’s Graduate School of Education, too, worries that in some regions private schools are the only route to a screen-free education, and that every student who opts out of public school takes funding with them. “What that looks like is fewer teachers, maybe a longer commute if a school were to close, and larger class sizes,” explained Garcia.

The parents with the means to leave, Garcia argues, are also the ones best equipped to change public schools for everyone else. “They have the social capital and resources, and they probably understand how to work within the bureaucratic system,” he said.

title: Excelencia in Education Certifies 21 Institutions

full_text:
Excelencia in Education has granted its 2026 Seal of Excelencia to 21 colleges and universities for “demonstrating continuous improvement in Latino, and all, student outcomes,” according to the organization.

The national network of educators and policymakers aims to use results-oriented higher education practices to “tap the talents of the Latino community” and meet workforce needs.

title: ‘Situated’ and Higher Ed Staff
summary:
‘Situated’ and Higher Ed Staff
joshua.m.kim@d… Tue, 10/27/2026 - 03:00 AM

Reading Angela Duckworth’s marvelous new book and thinking about Kevin McClure’s piece on the volatile higher ed workplace.

Byline(s)
Joshua Kim
full_text:
Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best by Angela Duckworth

Published in September 2026

Just as I was finishing Angela Duckworth’s marvelous new book, Situated, a piece by Kevin McClure called “Needlessly Insensitive Terminations in an Increasingly Volatile Higher Ed Workplace” crossed my radar. McClure, a professor of higher education at the University of North Carolina at Wilmington and author of The Caring University (2025), writes,

Situated is Duckworth’s companion piece and maybe somewhat of a correction (or at least an evolution) from her influential 2016 book, Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance. While I take no credit for Duckworth rounding out her thinking in Situated, I was gratified to read back to my 2016 piece “Could Grit Thinking Drive Inequality?”

In that critique, I was approaching Grit as a sociologist (my training), whereas for the psychologist Duckworth, context is more personal than structural. Still, nobody writes better about personal context than Duckworth. Situated is maybe the best book I’ve read about how we can exercise our individual agency to alter our immediate circumstances and environment and how effective these actions can be in shaping our life outcomes.

Throughout Situated, Duckworth offers numerous research-based stories and some deeply personal reflections about how our circumstances influence our thinking and behavior and how and where it is often more possible than we think to change our situations. The advice in Situated tends to focus on choices we can make in our immediate surroundings (including our work and home spaces), as well as on effective strategies for cultivating mentors, collaborators and reliable supporters.

None of the advice Duckworth offers is particularly radical. What is noteworthy, and one of the reasons why the book is so compelling, is Duckworth’s ability to integrate a broad range of research findings in showing how large a small change in context can have on individual flourishing.

All of this brings me back to the McClure piece. For higher ed staff, what might be the takeaways from reading Situated as they try to navigate an increasingly volatile employment environment? As McClure points out, most staff are at-will employees, meaning that “they can be let go for any reason or no reason at all.” How can a university staff member protect themselves from the vagaries of an insecure job if being gritty is ineffective—you can’t work your way into keeping a job if there is no money in the university budget—and there is no way to alter the situation of their institution’s declining financial situation?

One piece of advice Duckworth has is that we should all think about moving more—that finding a better situation sometimes requires changing one’s location, job and network. But is that really an option for most academic staff? Putting aside that households are not always portable—as partners have jobs and kids have schools and folks have caregiving obligations and community ties, etc., etc.—it is not clear that anyone would be safe moving to another university in another city or state. If McClure is right, and I expect he is, we are at the beginning of a trend toward both structural academic staff dislocations, accompanied by quiet firing techniques adopted from the corporate sector.

It may be that the best we can take from Situated is that higher ed staff should do whatever they can at their current institutions to influence their local environment. This means prioritizing work arrangements that reduce stress while increasing productivity, even if these changes require significant alterations to one’s daily routines and environment. If no higher ed staff job is secure, continuing to work in ways that prioritize the institution above the individual work makes less and less sense.

Would Duckworth—who, of course, has tenure—recommend to her academic staff colleagues that they should endeavor to build their work around their lives, rather than the other way around?

What are you reading?

title: How election officials are working to mitigate growing distrust ahead of midterms
summary: Election officials from coast to coast are facing a slew of challenges ahead of the high-stakes midterms.
full_text:
DALLAS, Ga. -- Election officials from coast to coast are facing a slew of challenges ahead of the high-stakes midterms, from the Trump administration's bid to impose itself on state-run elections to last-minute court challenges and threats faced by election workers -- all under a persistent sense of distrust in the voting process itself, some experts told ABC News.

"Usually the temperature is much higher -- and emotions run much hotter -- in a presidential election year than in a midterm election year," said Wendy Weiser, vice president of the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice at New York University School of Law. "This year, though, the temperature is staying up at a high level."

Election experts broadly lay blame for the elevated sense of distrust in elections this year at the feet of President Donald Trump, whose administration has taken unprecedented steps to question the outcome by levelling unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud.

Trump administration officials say steps they've taken in recent weeks -- including lawsuits in California and Alaska and threats to prosecute election workers -- are meant to ensure the integrity of the election.

But under the weight of those allegations, state officials say the once-collaborative rapport between the federal government and state leaders has in some cases given way to a deep sense of suspicion.

"There's no trust in that relationship," Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar told ABC News. "In order to have a working relationship, there has to be trust, and the fact that they continue to tear that trust apart and spread the misinformation and the lies that they are about our elections is wrong."

At the same time, people who oversee voting at the county level across the country are frequently fielding questions from voters who say they lack faith in the electoral process. About 6 in 10 Americans are confident the midterm elections will be conducted fairly and accurately, while nearly 4 in 10 Americans and about 3 in 10 voters are not confident , according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted using Ipsos' KnowledgePanel.

"No matter how transparent we are, people always are questioning what we're doing [and] how we're doing it," Deidre Holden, the director of elections and voter registration in Paulding County, Georgia, told ABC News. "I try to explain [that] we have nothing to hide. You're welcome to come in and watch the process."

'You never know what someone's going to do'

Holden, who has been an elections official in Georgia for 25 years, said that in her early years in the role, she "used to train people on how to smile and hand out an 'I voted' sticker."

Yet over the last several years, Holden has devoted much of her time to ensuring that everyone at polling places and in the county's ballot processing facility are safe. She currently has a sheriff's deputy stationed at every polling location, and in 2024 she first showed ABC News the active shooter training her poll workers were undertaking as a precaution.

"I'm forever concerned with the security of my staff, with my poll workers, with my voters," Holden said. "You never know what someone's going to do."

Paulding County was once a solidly Republican area, but as the suburban sprawl around Atlanta has increased, the county's population has quadrupled and it is now a purple county with Democrats and Republicans living side by side. With such a partisan divide, Holden said transparency about the process is key.

"Some of our best poll workers have come from the naysayers that didn't trust us and we invited them in and now they're our best workers and our biggest advocates because they get to see behind the scenes, they get see how the sausage is made, how we do things and how we do those things with integrity," Holden said.

'I just want to find 11,780 votes'

The official once again overseeing the election at the state level in Georgia this November is Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican who rose to national prominence in January 2021 after receiving a phone call from President Donald Trump.

"All I want to do is this: I just want to find 11,780 votes," Trump told Raffensperger at the time, claiming it was "not possible" that he lost Georgia's 2020 presidential election.

Joe Biden won the 2020 election in the Peach State and Raffensperger certified the results, despite facing criticism from some other Republicans.

"At the end of the day we did our job, we followed the law and we followed the constitution," Raffensperger told ABC News in a recent interview.

"I know I did the right thing, and I feel sorry for people that didn't do the right thing, because at some point, they're going to have to look at themselves in the mirror," he said.

Raffensperger's time in office will end in January. Early voting for the midterms is currently underway in Georgia, and Raffensperger said he is confident that residents will have an accurate idea of the projected election results by midnight after the polls close.

"Those ballots actually in effect will be counted three times just to verify the result, so at the end of the day, we know that the winner won and that's our job," Raffensperger said.

'What they've been able to uncover is nothing'

While Raffensperger was on the phone with Trump in 2021, many recent dustups between the federal government and state agencies have involved staffers going back and forth over email and video conferencing.

At the core of the growing friction is the claim by President Trump and DHS officials that the country has a "broken" election system, where they claim 278,000 people who are not U.S. citizens have registered to vote illegally.

Weiser told ABC News that the Trump administration has been attempting to "substantiate their theory that our country is plagued by widespread voter fraud."

"What they've been able to uncover is nothing," Weiser said. "Our elections, in fact, are safe and secure."

The allegations of widespread noncitizen voting have not just been made at press conferences. Over the summer, DHS employees reached out to states around the U.S., sending letters and holding meetings about "the concerning results" of what they called a "preliminary review" of potential noncitizens registered to vote.

Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state, said members of his office ended up on a video conference call in August with DHS representatives alleging that there could be as many as 15,903 noncitizens registered to vote in Nevada.

One of the DHS officials on the call was Heather Honey, a known election denier and a key figure in the fight to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

While not overtly hostile, a recording of the video conference obtained by ABC News shows palpable tension and some awkward exchanges, as Nevada officials seemed deeply skeptical of the claims made by DHS.

"So what you're saying is the 15,000 number has not been vetted?" a Nevada official asked, according to a recording of the video conference.

"I probably wouldn't use the sentence, 'It hasn't been vetted,'" a DHS representative responded, adding that each out has not "had a full manual review."

Following the meeting, DHS officials emailed Nevada officials with a new figure -- claiming they found 185 noncitizens on the state's voter rolls during a preliminary sweep. Officials in Nevada said the DHS was wrong, replying later that, after their own review of those 185 individuals, "our records indicate that they were citizens."

In response to a request by ABC News for comment, DHS stood by their work, which they called "a service to Nevada's citizens," and accused Nevada officials of knowingly harboring illegal voters on its lists.

"Nevada knows the 185 names they keep waving around were never the full list of illegal voters," a Homeland Security spokesperson said in an email. "They were only the files [that immigration officials] had finished reviewing at the moment of the call. Since then, [immigration officials] have manually confirmed about 2,000 more aliens from the same list. The review is just beginning."

Trusting the process

While voting in the upcoming election will conclude on Nov. 3, there is concern among some election experts that the relationship between federal leaders and their counterparts at the state and local levels might not be easily repairable.

The federal government has traditionally supported state and local officials on a slew of election-related matters, from mitigating foreign threats to cybersecurity. With the fragile state of affairs, some experts fear any Election Day complications could threaten the integrity of the vote.

"Our state and local election officials are going to have fewer resources at their disposal, less intelligence and less ability to coordinate in responding to what might be significant threats going forward because they don't trust the federal government as a partner the way they did," Weiser said.

While trust in how elections are being conducted remains top of mind for voters, election officials like Holden, Aguilar and Raffensperger are working to assure their residents that they should still have faith in the process.

"There's no reason for a voter to ever doubt their ballot," Holden said.

title: IEAA Excellence Awards 2026: Winners announced
summary:
The best of Australia’s international education industry were celebrated at the IEAA Excellence Awards, held during the 40th Australian International Education Conference (AIEC) in Sydney.

The post IEAA Excellence Awards 2026: Winners announced appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The Excellence Awards, which are held annually, celebrate the contributions of individuals and teams developing Australia’s reputation for quality and innovation in international education. The awards span leadership, best practice, innovation, research, and the rising stars of the next generation.

Simon Ridings, who began as a tutor and PhD candidate at the University of Queensland, took the accolade for ‘Distinguished Contribution to International Education.’ Recognised for his broad contribution to Australia’s international education across three decades, six universities and the sector’s largest professional body – IEAA – his work has benefitted not only international students, but also the professionals who serve them.

Serving as the IEAA vice-president and president from 2020 to 2024, he helped grow the organisation’s membership, expand its professional development, and strengthened its research.

Ren Yi, president of IEAA, said the winners “represent the best Australia has to offer the world of education,” adding that the organisation is proud to highlight the accomplishments within the community.

“From innovative programs which elevate the student experience, to outstanding examples of leadership, the winners and commendations once again demonstrate how much impact individuals can have on international education as a whole,” he said.

The platform miXabroad won the ‘Innovation in International Education’ award for producing a global benchmark for learning abroad. The framework, developed by researchers and university practitioners across Australia, the UK, Europe and the US, allows institutions to benchmark student experience and impact across programs, cohorts and countries by connecting student voices and comparative evidence.

This evidence base has helped highlight the value of global mobility and the role it plays in creating adaptable, resilient and globally capable graduates at a time when international education is being challenged.

“Even as the sector is buffeted by policy shifts and political pressure, these leaders continue to adapt and innovate in the service of our world-leading international education industry, ” said Phil Honeywood, CEO of IEAA.

“The award winners and commendations demonstrate the depth of talent in Australia, and how international education continues to transform lives, one student at a time,” he said.

title: AIEC at 40: Australian international education looks to its next chapter
summary:
International education leaders have gathered in Sydney for the 40th Australian International Education Conference (AIEC), with policy uncertainty, shifting student mobility and AI setting the backdrop for four days of debate about where the sector goes next.

The post AIEC at 40: Australian international education looks to its next chapter appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
More than four decades after the conference first brought the industry together, AIEC 2026 opened on October 27 under the theme “Future Thinking”.

Policy settings across major study destinations have tightened, student behaviours are changing and institutions are looking increasingly towards transnational education and new markets for growth. Meanwhile, AI is rapidly reshaping how prospective students discover, compare and choose their education.

Opening the conference remotely, Australian education minister Jason Clare sought to put the focus back on the impact of international education beyond its economic contribution.

“International education employs a lot of Australians. It makes an important contribution to our economy. But it does more than that,” Clare told delegates.

“It also connects us to the world.”

His comments came as Australia continues to recalibrate its own international education settings after several years of policy upheaval and efforts to slow migration and international student growth.

Clare acknowledged the “big challenges” facing the sector and said the government was working with industry to put it on a “more sustainable path”, while defending measures introduced to strengthen integrity, target unscrupulous operators and improve student protection.

But his speech also pointed towards one of the major themes emerging for Australian education: taking more of it offshore.

Five Australian universities have recently opened campuses in India, Clare said, with Western Sydney University preparing to open in Greater Noida. Vietnam has also approved an investment licence for RMIT’s new Hanoi campus.

“Not everyone can come here to study. Not everyone can afford it. But we can come to them,” he said.

That shift towards transnational education is among the topics on the agenda at AIEC this week, alongside AI, international talent and changing student expectations.

For IDP Education CEO and managing director Tennealle O’Shannessy, the conference’s 40th anniversary provides an opportunity to consider just how far the sector has travelled and how quickly it may need to change again.

International education looks very different today than it did 40 years ago. That evolution isn’t slowing down, and we need to come together to plan for the changes ahead, whether they’re driven by technology or policy.

Tennealle O’Shannessy, IDP

“International education looks very different today than it did 40 years ago,” said O’Shannessy.

“That evolution isn’t slowing down, and we need to come together to plan for the changes ahead, whether they’re driven by technology or policy.”

International Education Association of Australia (IEAA) CEO Phil Honeywood said the 40th anniversary was an opportunity to reflect on the sector’s evolution while looking ahead to what comes next.

“Shifts in geopolitics and policy will continue to force evolution in our sector, but there is an opportunity for us to take greater control of our future,” said Honeywood.

“That requires collaboration across institutions, industry and government, and AIEC is the perfect time to come together and align on our priorities into the future.”

The anniversary comes at a particularly consequential time for Australia, where international education remains both a major export industry and a recurring focus of the political debate around migration, housing and sustainable growth.

Clare, however, used the opening to emphasise the human story behind those debates. He told delegates about an Afghan woman who escaped Kabul and has now begun a PhD in Australia while her sister remains in Afghanistan, where women and girls face severe restrictions on education.

He reminded delegates of the “transformational power of education”.

Co-hosted by IDP Education and the IEAA, AIEC runs from October 27–30 at Sydney’s International Convention Centre.

The PIE News is a media partner for AIEC 2026 and will be reporting from Sydney throughout the conference.

title: Can the UK achieve its international education strategy ambitions under the current BCA framework?
summary:
Following the debate on the recruitment consequences of BCA reform, BUILA chair Stuart Easter considers the changes needed to support effective compliance and the UK’s wider international education ambitions.

The post Can the UK achieve its international education strategy ambitions under the current BCA framework? appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Alex Lock and Mike Strong’s recent article in The PIE highlighted the potential consequences of the Basic Compliance Assessment framework for recruitment diversity and institutional resilience. Their analysis highlights the need to consider what changes would enable institutions to fulfil their sponsor responsibilities while continuing to deliver the objectives of the international education strategy.

BUILA supports a robust compliance framework that protects the integrity of the student route and maintains public confidence in international education. Our members recognise their responsibilities to assess applicants appropriately, oversee recruitment relationships and support students through enrolment and study.

For institutions to discharge those responsibilities effectively, they need a transparent and consistent basis for understanding risk, timely information about visa outcomes and an opportunity to address concerns.

These conditions also matter for the international education strategy’s commitment to sustainable recruitment of high-quality international students from a diverse range of countries. Institutions’ capacity to maintain that breadth of recruitment depends, in part, on their confidence in the framework within which they operate.

Information to support effective compliance

Where a visa application is refused, institutions need sufficient information to understand whether the decision identifies a weakness in their recruitment or admissions processes and what action would address it.

This is particularly important where refusals relate to assessments of an applicant’s credibility. Sponsors need to distinguish between circumstances specific to an applicant, shortcomings in their own checks and wider changes in how risk is being assessed.

Without that understanding, additional interviews or documentary requirements may increase the demands on applicants and institutions without resolving the underlying concern.

More timely Home Office data sharing, alongside greater transparency about the indicators used to assess applicant risk, would support better-informed decisions before a Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies is issued. It would also enable institutions to review the effectiveness of their interventions and respond to emerging concerns during the recruitment cycle.

The value of that information depends on its timeliness and level of detail. Where institutions cannot confidently assess the risks associated with recruitment activity, restricting that activity may become the most immediate means of protecting their sponsor position.

Access to actionable intelligence would provide a stronger basis for maintaining responsible recruitment across a diverse range of markets, consistent with the ambitions of the international education strategy.

A proportionate response to emerging concerns

The use of red, amber and green ratings should provide a clear basis for identifying concerns and supporting improvement.

BUILA recommends that amber ratings operate as internal early-warning indicators, prompting dialogue with UKVI and an opportunity for institutions to take corrective action where required. Sponsors should understand the concern being raised, the improvement expected and how that improvement will be assessed.

If an amber rating automatically triggers sanctions or public reputational consequences, institutions may feel compelled to restrict recruitment before they have had sufficient opportunity to understand and address the issue. This risks reducing legitimate recruitment without establishing whether the underlying processes have improved.

An approach that enables early intervention would maintain institutional accountability while supporting the sustainable recruitment envisaged by the international education strategy. It would also provide a clearer basis for assessing whether corrective action has addressed the risks identified.

The implications of publishing institutional ratings

Publishing institution-level ratings requires consideration of how those measures may be interpreted beyond their regulatory purpose.

A sponsor compliance rating measures a particular set of outcomes. Prospective students, families and overseas partners may nevertheless interpret it as a broader judgement about an institution’s academic quality or its reliability as a place to study.

The consequences could extend beyond individual institutions to Brand UK. If ratings undermine confidence in UK universities, they could influence students’ choice of destination and overseas partners’ willingness to collaborate. This would work against the international education strategy’s ambitions for sustainable, diversified recruitment and stronger international relationships.

BUILA has therefore asked that institution-level red, amber and green ratings remain unpublished; at a minimum, amber ratings should remain internal. The potential consequences for recruitment, international partnerships and Brand UK should form part of government’s assessment of publication, alongside its intended regulatory benefits.

Stabilisation and coordinated policy assessment

A period of policy stabilisation would allow the effects of the reforms to be assessed and effective data-sharing arrangements to be established. BUILA is seeking a pause in further changes and RAG-related sanctions while this work takes place.

The assessment should consider whether institutional responses are improving recruitment practice or primarily reducing exposure to outcomes that sponsors cannot readily anticipate. A reduction in recruitment does not demonstrate that the underlying compliance concerns have been resolved.

This requires coordinated engagement between the Home Office and the government departments responsible for international education, working with the sector. Their assessment should consider the consequences for genuine applicants, recruitment diversity, international partnerships and institutional sustainability, alongside sponsor performance.

Evidence from institutions’ international recruitment, admissions and compliance teams should inform that dialogue, ensuring that policy assessment reflects both the responsibilities sponsors hold and the practical circumstances in which they make decisions.

Supporting the UK’s international education ambitions

BUILA is seeking timely visa-outcome data, greater transparency about applicant risk, a proportionate approach to the use and publication of institutional ratings and sufficient time to assess the effects of the reforms.

These changes would give institutions a more dependable basis for meeting their sponsor responsibilities while maintaining international student recruitment across a diverse range of countries. They would also support greater alignment between the compliance framework, and the international education objectives Government has set.

As both chair of BUILA and a university director, I recognise the responsibility on institutions to maintain effective recruitment and compliance arrangements.

Our ability to fulfil that responsibility depends on access to the information needed to understand concerns and take appropriate action. Ensuring those conditions are in place would strengthen sponsor practice while supporting the UK’s reputation and its capacity to deliver the international education strategy.

The post From Classroom to Career: An AI-Enhanced Scaffolded Job Interview Approach in the L2 Classroom appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
It is widely recognized among language instructors that effective second language teaching involves more than presenting grammar rules and vocabulary in isolation. Instead, meaningful learning develops when instructional activities connect to learners’ realities and lived experiences, enabling them to use the language to interpret, express, and negotiate meaning in contexts that matter to them. When classroom tasks reflect familiar situations—such as interacting in professional environments, navigating institutions, participating in multilingual communities, and communicating in person or through digital platforms—students engage more fully and demonstrate greater retention (Sujarwati, Iis et al.; Pérez-Núñez; Safarova). In these contexts, language functions not as an abstract object of study but as a communicative practice embedded in social life.

Building on this perspective, research in second language acquisition further shows that learning is strengthened when new linguistic knowledge is connected to prior experience (Vishnyakova et al.; Gajo; Müller; Mór). Learners interpret and retain language more effectively when forms are introduced through meaningful contexts that invite reflection, interaction, and purposeful expression. This understanding is so widely accepted in the field that the ACTFL World-Readiness Standards for Learning Languages reinforce it, emphasizing communication in real-world contexts and the development of intercultural competence. Together, these principles have shaped curricular design across proficiency levels, encouraging instructional practices that situate language within authentic communicative environments.

Within this broader pedagogical framework, textbooks and curricula often attempt to reflect learners’ daily lives by incorporating scenarios related to routines, social interactions, and academic experiences. As proficiency increases, students develop the linguistic range necessary to describe their perspectives with greater precision and complexity, engaging with disciplinary content such as literature, cultural analysis, or professional communication. However, despite this progression toward authenticity, one context that remains underutilized across the broader curriculum is the job interview (Calvo; Louw; Zekeri).

To address this gap, this article proposes the incorporation of job interview preparation and role-play activities beginning at the Spanish high-intermediate level and continuing into advanced courses, integrating reading, writing, and speaking within a communicative task that students perceive as both immediate and consequential. As learners approach graduation, their professional goals become more defined, and the need to articulate their experiences, strengths, and aspirations in the target language becomes increasingly relevant. In response, this article presents a scaffolded job interview activity designed to foster linguistic development, cultural reflection, and professional confidence across proficiency levels, allowing students to progressively refine their communicative strategies over time.

At the initial stage, students are introduced to core interview vocabulary and conventions through short video clips that illustrate a range of communicative styles. Selected excerpts from Spanish-language media, along with dubbed scenes from familiar television series—such as Betty la Fea and The Office (including hilarious Dwight’s job interviews in Spanish dubbing)—serve as accessible entry points for discussion. These materials function as conversational catalysts, encouraging students to analyze effective responses, identify common interview questions, and reflect on their own experiences. In classrooms characterized by diverse linguistic backgrounds and professional trajectories, these discussions often generate rich exchanges about expectations, challenges, and strategies for professional self-presentation.

As the activity progresses, students are introduced to structured approaches for responding to behavioral interview questions. One example is the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result), which provides a clear framework for organizing responses to prompts such as describing a professional challenge or explaining how a problem was resolved. Always in Spanish, Students analyze sample responses, examine how narrative structure contributes to clarity and persuasiveness, and begin constructing their own answers. At this stage, the focus extends beyond linguistic accuracy to rhetorical effectiveness, encouraging students to present their experiences in a coherent and compelling manner.

In addition, this stage prepares students to engage more critically and purposefully with ChatGPT in the following phase of the activity, which is completed as a guided homework assignment. In this simulation, students use artificial intelligence as both interviewer and language support tool, engaging in a structured practice interview outside the classroom. The instructions, originally written in Spanish, are provided below in translation for broader accessibility.

Guided Homework Activity: Job Interview Practice with ChatGPT

As part of this activity, the student will conduct a job interview in Spanish at home using ChatGPT. The goal is to strengthen speaking skills, expand vocabulary, and build confidence in professional communication before moving on to in-class role plays. Below are the instructions provided to the student.

Step 1: Choose a Position and Workplace

Select a job that interests you—your “dream job.” Be as specific as possible about both the position and the place where you would like to work (for example, the type of institution, organization, or company, and its location or context).

Step 2: Prepare Your Profile in Spanish

Write a short preparation note including:

The name of the position

A brief description of the job (2–3 sentences)

Three skills or experiences that make you a strong candidate

Information about the company or institution

Your professional and educational background

Step 3: Simulated Interview with ChatGPT

Copy and paste the following prompt into ChatGPT (you may adapt it to your chosen position):

“Act as an interviewer for a position as [job title] at [company, hospital, or institution]. The interview will be conducted in Spanish. Ask me between 5 and 7 typical job interview questions for this position. After each of my responses, provide brief corrections or comments on how I can improve my expression, grammar, or vocabulary. Use a formal tone, as in a real job interview.”

During the simulation:

Respond orally to each question (you may use the microphone feature to record your answers).

Respond as naturally as possible, as if in a real interview.

Carefully review the feedback provided by ChatGPT after each response.

Use the suggestions to refine subsequent answers.

Save useful feedback for future reference.

At the end, save the full transcript of your interview, including both responses and feedback.

After the simulation:

Review your responses and ChatGPT’s feedback carefully.

Write a revised version of your answers, incorporating improvements where appropriate.

Read your revised responses aloud to practice pronunciation and fluency.

Be prepared to share insights and key takeaways in our in-class discussion.

Classroom Implementation and Student Impact

This is the fourth semester in which I have incorporated a ChatGPT-based component into a job interview activity that I have developed and refined over several years. Student feedback has been consistently positive, particularly regarding the value of AI-generated feedback in helping them refine their responses and develop more precise, context-appropriate vocabulary. Many students also note that practicing in a lower-anxiety, interactive environment increases their confidence, especially when they later participate in in-class role plays where they alternate roles as interviewer and candidate.

In the third segment of the activity, students first work in pairs in the classroom and then continue collaborating outside of class over the course of a week as they prepare for a final in-class simulation: a “grand finale” interview in which they apply for a position aligned with their professional aspirations. After each performance, classmates identify strengths and effective strategies demonstrated by their peers, while suggestions for improvement are offered in general terms to support collective reflection and ongoing learning at the end of all presentations.

As mentioned earlier, I typically implement this activity first in high-intermediate Spanish courses and then revisit it in advanced-level courses. This progression across semesters reveals noticeable gains in fluency, confidence, and professional discourse. In advanced courses, it is not uncommon for students to be actively applying for real positions while completing the activity. Many report feeling significantly more comfortable articulating their skills, experiences, and goals in interview settings, often noting that the transfer from Spanish to English interview contexts feels unexpectedly seamless.

Although the controlled classroom environment cannot fully replicate the unpredictability of real interviews, many of the most common questions—such as describing oneself, discussing experience, articulating strengths and weaknesses, explaining motivation, or imagining future goals—remain consistent across contexts. Because students recognize the direct relevance of these tasks, engagement increases substantially. As one student remarked, this is “useful stuff,” a comment that captures the pedagogical value of aligning language learning with authentic communicative needs. My experience in the classroom has also been echoed in the work of other instructors who have implemented similar activities in different disciplinary contexts. Calvo-Benzies (2021) in the field of tourism, notes that learners often “crave” the practical application offered by job interview simulations, as these tasks provide a tangible sense of reality while developing transferable professional skills that extend beyond the classroom. Such findings reinforce the relevance and longevity of this type of instructional design.

For this reason, repeating the job interview activity across consecutive courses creates an additional layer of development, allowing students not only to improve but also to recognize their own progress over time. This visible trajectory of growth strengthens confidence, reinforces motivation, and deepens students’ sense of agency as multilingual speakers capable of navigating real-world professional spaces in more than one language.

Ultimately, we as faculty are part of the growth and development not only of our subject of expertise but also of well-rounded human beings whom we hope to support and see succeed. Teaching language, in this sense, is teaching for life itself: it is about the joys of what students will go on to accomplish, the confidence they will carry forward, and the meaningful ways they will use their voices in the world beyond the classroom.

Angela Rodriguez Mooney, PhD, is an assistant professor of Spanish and the Texas Women’s University.

summary:
